name: Pew Research Center on Public and Expert Views of AI
title: Pew Research Center on Public and Expert Views of AI
answer: Pew Research Center publishes survey research on how the U.S. public, AI experts and global populations view artificial intelligence, including its effects on work, information and human connection. Its most useful finding for faith organisations is a widening gap between expert optimism and public concern, with about half of U.S. adults more concerned than excited about AI in daily life while experts are far more positive.

sections.body: Pew Research Center is a non-partisan fact tank that publishes survey reports, short reads and methodological studies on public opinion. The pages read here span 2018 to 2026 and cover American and global attitudes toward artificial intelligence, expert canvassings, and a 2026 test of whether AI models can stand in for human survey respondents. The material is research rather than guidance for congregations, and no page addresses churches or faith organisations directly.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Across five years of surveys Pew finds the American public steadily more wary of AI while experts remain more optimistic. In a 2025 report comparing the two groups, 56 percent of experts said AI would have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years against 17 percent of the public, and 47 percent of experts were more excited than concerned about AI in daily life against 11 percent of adults. Half of adults were more concerned than excited, up from about four in ten in 2021 and 2022. Both groups worried about inaccurate information, with seven in ten experts and 66 percent of adults highly worried. A 2026 report found about half of adults now use AI chatbots, roughly a quarter daily, with 38 percent of employed adults using them for work and one in ten for emotional support. Teens were heavier users still, and about six in ten said students at their school use chatbots to cheat at least somewhat often. A 2026 global survey of 42,151 people in 36 countries found people in 34 of 37 countries expected AI to reduce rather than increase jobs. A methodological study concluded AI models are not yet an adequate replacement for traditional polling.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Pew surveyed 5,410 U.S. adults in August 2024 and 1,013 AI experts between August and October 2024. It surveyed 5,119 U.S. adults in February 2026 and 42,151 people across 36 countries between February and May 2026. It reports 56 percent of experts against 17 percent of the public expecting positive national impact, 51 percent of adults more concerned than excited against 15 percent of experts, 57 percent of adults against 37 percent of experts fearing loss of human connection, and 64 percent of teens ages 13 to 17 using an AI chatbot.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: The surveys give clergy and congregational leaders a documented picture of the people in their pews. The public arrives at AI with more concern than excitement, particular worry about lost human connection and inaccurate information, and growing everyday use of chatbots, including for emotional support. The finding that one in ten adults turns to chatbots for emotional support is directly relevant to pastoral care, and the teen figures speak to youth ministry and questions of honesty in schoolwork. The expert-public gap also explains why technologists and congregations often talk past each other.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: Pew measures opinion, not practice, and none of the pages read addresses churches, clergy or religious institutions as such, so any application to ministry is inference rather than finding. The reports are snapshots at different dates with different samples and question wordings, so figures are not always directly comparable. The synthetic survey study is a methodological test of Pew's own polling, not a statement about AI in religious settings.
